impute

/im-PYOOT/ - rhymes with dispute · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Impute means to attribute or assign blame for something to someone.

Historians still impute the treaty's collapse to the young interpreter, though the archives tell a messier story.

Example

When the bakery's cakes came out sunken for a week straight, the owner imputed the failures to the new oven boy — until the flour supplier admitted changing the blend.

Impute is the formal verb for laying blame at someone's door, often on thin proof, and it keeps a fixed frame: you impute something to someone. Blame is the everyday word; accuse charges a person openly, while impute can work quietly, in reports and rumors.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

assign: Assign is the plain, neutral verb for allotting fault or credit — a report assigns responsibility and moves on. Impute is heavier and more suspicious: it books blame to someone's account, often on thin proof, always in the frame impute something to someone.

pin: To pin the blame on somebody is the informal version — quick and casual, and it always takes on. Impute does the same job in formal dress: courts and historians impute a failure to a person, and the word hints the proof may be thin.

charge: To charge someone is to declare them at fault out loud and on the record — an open accusation made to their face. Impute can work quietly, at a distance, in reports and rumors; the blame may never be spoken to the person at all.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

excuse: to lift blame away instead of laying it on

clear: to free someone of suspicion entirely

Where it sits · how directly the blame is laid

hint → impute → accuse

hint vs. impute: A hint merely gestures at who might be at fault — it stops far short of impute, which formally lays the blame at someone's door.

accuse vs. impute: Accuse goes further than impute: imputing assigns fault, often at a distance and in writing, while accusing charges the person openly to their face.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — im-: in, onto (a form of in-)

Root — -pute: to reckon, to settle an account (Latin putare)

Put it together: The im- is the directional in- — 'onto' — not a negation: im- + putare ('to reckon, to settle an account') is to enter a debt onto someone's ledger. Impute still works exactly that way: the fault is booked to a name. Putare also gives compute and reputation.

Use the root in a new word: compute: By lamplight the clerk computed the season's earnings down to the last penny.
